subject.title: Labour and Industrial Law - I
subject.description: Constitutional framework of labour protection, industrial dispute resolution under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, economic coercion mechanisms, statutory closure procedures, and Gujarat Industrial Relations Act. Total Marks: 100. Credits: 5.

subject.title: Labour and Industrial Law - II
subject.description: Workplace safety, health, and welfare under the Factories Act, 1948, minimum and fair wages statutes, and social security enactments (ESI, Gratuity, EPF, and Employees Compensation). Total Marks: 100. Credits: 5.

subject.title: Principles of Taxation Laws
subject.description: Constitutional basis of taxation, Income Tax Act, 1961 fundamentals, five heads of income, deductions, assessment procedures, and Goods and Services Tax (GST) architecture. Total Marks: 100. Credits: 5.

subject.title: Principal of Banking Laws
subject.description: Evolution of banking institutions, Reserve Bank of India regulation, Banking Regulation Act, 1949, banker-customer relationship, negotiable instruments, debt recovery tribunals, and electronic banking. Total Marks: 100. Credits: 5.

subject.title: Information Technology Laws and Cyber Crimes
subject.description: Cyber law architecture under the Information Technology Act, 2000, digital signatures, electronic governance, computer crimes, civil penalties, cyber forensics, and data protection jurisprudence. Total Marks: 100. Credits: 5.

unit.description: Writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 & 226, and fundamental duties.

unit.description: Definition of crime, Actus Reus, Mens Rea, and punishments.

unit.title: Offences Affecting Human Body
unit.description: Homicide, murder, mob lynching, and causing hurt.

unit.title: Offences Against Women & Children

unit.title: Offences Against Property & State

unit.description: Lawful consideration and capacity to enter into agreements.

unit.title: Void Agreements & Breach

unit.title: Strict & Absolute Liability

unit.description: Civil negligence, duty of care, and defamation standards.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Define "State" under Article 12 of the Constitution of India.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Define "State" under Article 12 of the Constitution of India. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer: Under Article 12, "State" includes: (1) The Government and Parliament of India, (2) The Government and Legislature of each State, (3) All local authorities (e.g., Municipalities, Panchayats), and (4) Other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India. In Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib, the Supreme Court laid down that if a body is financially, functionally, and administratively dominated by the Government, it is an instrumentality of the State under Article 12.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: What is the "Doctrine of Severability" under Article 13(1)?
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: What is the "Doctrine of Severability" under Article 13(1)? (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer: The Doctrine of Severability (Art 13) provides that when a statute violates fundamental rights, only the unconstitutional portion is void, provided the valid and invalid portions are separable. If the valid part can independently survive and operate without the invalid portion, the court will uphold the valid part (A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras; R.M.D.C. v. Union of India).

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Explain the "Golden Triangle" of Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Explain the "Golden Triangle" of Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Introduction: Articles 14 (Equality), 19 (Basic Freedoms), and 21 (Right to Life & Personal Liberty) form the "Golden Triangle" of the Indian Constitution.
2. Doctrinal Shift: Earlier in A.K. Gopalan (1950), the Supreme Court held these articles were mutually exclusive compartments. This was overruled in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978).
3. Interconnection: In Maneka Gandhi, Bhagwati J. ruled that a law depriving a person of life or personal liberty under Article 21 must also satisfy the test of Article 19 (reasonable restrictions) and Article 14 (non-arbitrariness). The "procedure established by law" must be "just, fair, and reasonable" and not whimsical.
4. Conclusion: The Golden Triangle serves as the foundational bulwark against arbitrary executive and legislative action, infusing substantive due process into Indian constitutional jurisprudence.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Discuss the scope and grounds of judicial review of Constitutional Amendments under the Basic Structure Doctrine.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Discuss the scope and grounds of judicial review of Constitutional Amendments under the Basic Structure Doctrine. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Introduction:
Article 368 empowers Parliament to amend the Constitution. However, this power is constituent and plenary, not unlimited. The Basic Structure Doctrine acts as an implied constitutional limitation to preserve core democratic principles.

2. Historical Evolution:
- Shankari Prasad (1951) & Sajjan Singh (1965): Upheld absolute parliamentary power under Article 368.
- Golaknath (1967): Held Parliament cannot abridge Fundamental Rights under Part III.
- 24th Amendment (1971): Parliament amended Art 13 & 368 to assert unrestricted power.

3. Landmark Ruling — Kesavananda Bharati (1973):
A 13-judge bench held by 7:6 majority that while Parliament can amend any provision of the Constitution, including Part III, it cannot alter, abrogate, or destroy the "Basic Structure" of the Constitution.

4. Recognized Basic Features:
(a) Supremacy of the Constitution
(b) Republican and Democratic form of Government
(c) Secular character of the Constitution
(d) Separation of Powers between Legislature, Executive, and Judiciary
(e) Federal character of the Constitution
(f) Judicial Review (L. Chandra Kumar, 1997)
(g) Harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles (Minerva Mills, 1980)

5. Subsequent Affirmations:
In Minerva Mills (1980), clauses (4) and (5) of Art 368 were struck down. In the NJAC Case (2015), the 99th Constitutional Amendment was nullified because it compromised judicial independence.

6. Conclusion:
The Basic Structure Doctrine maintains constitutional equilibrium, ensuring Parliament cannot use its amendatory power to subvert constitutional democracy.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Examine the scope of Right to Equality under Article 14 of the Constitution. Distinguish between Reasonable Classification Test and the Doctrine of Non-Arbitrariness.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Examine the scope of Right to Equality under Article 14 of the Constitution. Distinguish between Reasonable Classification Test and the Doctrine of Non-Arbitrariness. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Introduction & Constitutional Framework:
Article 14 declares that "The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India."
- Equality before Law: A negative concept borrowed from English Common Law, implying absence of special privilege.
- Equal Protection of Laws: A positive concept borrowed from the 14th Amendment of the US Constitution, requiring equal treatment under equal circumstances ("equals must be treated equally, unequals cannot be treated equally").

2. Traditional Doctrine: Reasonable Classification:
Since absolute equality among unequal persons creates inequality, Article 14 permits legislative classification. In State of W.B. v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952) and Ram Krishna Dalmia (1958), the Supreme Court established the two-fold test:
(i) Intelligible Differentia: The classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia distinguishing persons or things grouped together from others left out.
(ii) Rational Nexus: The differentia must have a rational relation/nexus to the object sought to be achieved by the statute.

3. The Modern Dimension: Doctrine of Non-Arbitrariness:
In E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974), Bhagwati J. revolutionized Article 14 jurisprudence:
"Equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects and dimensions... Equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies; one belongs to the rule of law in a republic while the other, to the whim and caprice of an absolute monarch."
This was affirmed in Maneka Gandhi (1978) and Ramana Dayaram Shetty (1979).

4. Evolution into "Manifest Arbitrariness":
In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court held that "manifest arbitrariness" is a valid constitutional ground to strike down even primary legislation. A law is manifestly arbitrary if enacted without adequate determining principle or is excessively disproportionate, unreasonable, or capricious.

5. Comparison between Classification and Arbitrariness:
- Classification is a formulaic tool to assess statutory boundaries.
- Non-arbitrariness is the substantive core of Rule of Law ensuring fairness in state action.

6. Conclusion:
Article 14 has progressed from a formalistic classification test into an activist, substantive guarantee against unfairness, executive caprice, and legislative oppression.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Problem Question: The State Government issues an executive notification reserving 80% of management quota seats in private unaided law colleges exclusively for students domiciled in Gujarat. A meritorious student from Rajasthan challenging this notification claims violation of Articles 14, 15, and 19(1)(g). Decide using the IRAC method.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Problem Question: The State Government issues an executive notification reserving 80% of management quota seats in private unaided law colleges exclusively for students domiciled in Gujarat. A meritorious student from Rajasthan challenging this notification claims violation of Articles 14, 15, and 19(1)(g). Decide using the IRAC method. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
LEGAL PROBLEM ANALYSIS (IRAC METHOD)

1. ISSUES:
(a) Whether an 80% institutional/domicile quota in private unaided professional colleges violates the Right to Equality under Article 14.
(b) Whether the State executive notification impermissibly infringes the private colleges' right to occupation under Article 19(1)(g).
(c) Whether the Rajasthan petitioner is entitled to relief.

2. RELEVANT RULES & CONSTITUTIONAL PRINCIPLES:
- Article 14: Prohibits arbitrary state classification lacking rational nexus.
- Article 19(1)(g): Protects freedom to practice any profession or carry on any occupation/trade.
- P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005): A 7-judge bench ruled that the State cannot impose reservation policy or quota system on private unaided educational institutions.
- Dr. Pradeep Jain v. Union of India (1984): Excessive domicile reservation destroying merit violates Article 14.

3. APPLICATION TO FACTS:
- The private law colleges are unaided institutions. Under the P.A. Inamdar precedent, the state has no authority to commandeer 80% seats under an executive order.
- Furthermore, an 80% domicile reservation is excessively disproportionate and fails the rational nexus test, virtually barring outside meritorious candidates.
- Domicile preference cannot exceed reasonable ceilings (as held in Pradeep Jain).

4. CONCLUSION:
The executive notification is ultra vires Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The petition of the candidate from Rajasthan will succeed, and the 80% domicile quota must be quashed.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: What constitutes "Community Service" as a new form of punishment under Section 4(f) of BNS 2023?
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: What constitutes "Community Service" as a new form of punishment under Section 4(f) of BNS 2023? (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer: Section 4(f) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS 2023) introduces "Community Service" as a distinct form of punishment. It requires convicted offenders in petty offences (such as theft of property under ₹5,000 upon return under Sec 303(2) proviso, public servant unlawful business Sec 202, or first-time defamation Sec 356) to perform unpaid beneficial work for the community under court supervision.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Define "Organized Crime" under Section 111 of BNS 2023.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Explain the offence of "Terrorist Act" under Section 113 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS 2023).
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Explain the offence of "Terrorist Act" under Section 113 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS 2023). (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Statutory Framework: Section 113 of BNS 2023 incorporates the offence of "Terrorist Act" into general penal law.
2. Essential Elements: An act is a terrorist act if done with intent to threaten or likely to threaten the unity, integrity, sovereignty, security, or economic security of India, or with intent to strike terror in the people or any section thereof.
3. Means Employed: Using bombs, dynamite, firearms, lethal weapons, poisonous gases, radioactive materials, or destroying critical infrastructure/monetary stability.
4. Penal Sanctions:
- If the terrorist act results in death: Punishable with Death or Imprisonment for Life, and minimum fine of ₹10 Lakhs.
- In other cases: Imprisonment from 5 years up to Life Imprisonment, with fine.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Distinguish between Murder (Section 101 BNS / Sec 300 IPC) and Culpable Homicide not amounting to Murder (Section 100 BNS / Sec 299 IPC) with landmark judicial tests.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Distinguish between Murder (Section 101 BNS / Sec 300 IPC) and Culpable Homicide not amounting to Murder (Section 100 BNS / Sec 299 IPC) with landmark judicial tests. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Genus vs Species Relationship:
All murders are culpable homicides, but all culpable homicides are not murder. Culpable homicide (Sec 100 BNS / Sec 299 IPC) is the genus, while Murder (Sec 101 BNS / Sec 300 IPC) is the species.

2. The Fundamental Distinction — Probability of Death:
In the classic ruling Reg. v. Govinda (1876), Melvill J. established that the line of demarcation depends upon the degree of risk to human life:

(A) Intention:
- Culpable Homicide (Sec 100): Intention to cause death OR intention to cause bodily injury likely to cause death.
- Murder (Sec 101): Intention to cause death OR intention to cause bodily injury which offender knows is likely to cause death OR intention to inflict bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death (Virsa Singh test).

(B) Knowledge:
- Culpable Homicide: Knowledge that the act is likely to cause death.
- Murder (4th Clause): Knowledge that the act is so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death, without any excuse.

3. The 5 Exceptions to Murder:
An act prima facie falling under Section 101 BNS is reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder if covered by any of the 5 exceptions:
(i) Grave and sudden provocation
(ii) Exceeding the right of private defence in good faith
(iii) Public servant exceeding lawful powers in good faith
(iv) Sudden fight in heat of passion without premeditation
(v) Victim above 18 years consenting to suffer death

4. Conclusion:
Culpable homicide is punishable under Sec 105 BNS (Imprisonment up to 10 yrs or Life), whereas Murder is punishable under Sec 103 BNS (Death or Life Imprisonment).

examPrepQuestion.questionText: What is a "Cross Offer"? Does it result in a binding contract?
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: What is a "Cross Offer"? Does it result in a binding contract? (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer: A Cross Offer occurs when two parties make identical offers to each other in ignorance of the other's offer simultaneously. Cross offers do not constitute acceptance of each other because there is no consensus ad idem (meeting of minds). Hence, cross offers do not result in a binding contract (Tinn v. Hoffman & Co., 1873).

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Explain the doctrine of "Promissory Estoppel" in Indian Contract Law.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Explain the doctrine of "Promissory Estoppel" in Indian Contract Law. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Definition: Promissory Estoppel is an equitable doctrine providing that where one party makes a clear promise intending to create legal relations, and the other party acts upon it and alters their position, the promisor cannot go back on the promise.
2. Key Elements:
(a) Clear and unambiguous representation or promise.
(b) Reasonable reliance and alteration of position by the promisee.
(c) Inequity if promisor is permitted to resile.
3. Application to Government: In Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills (1979), Bhagwati J. held that promissory estoppel applies against the Government where executive promises induced citizens to set up industries or invest capital, unless overriding public interest justifies otherwise.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Discuss the Doctrine of Frustration of Contract under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. State the grounds and exceptions.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Discuss the Doctrine of Frustration of Contract under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. State the grounds and exceptions. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Statutory Framework:
Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act provides:
- An agreement to do an impossible act is void ab initio.
- A contract becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful after the contract is made without the default of the promisor (Supervening Impossibility / Frustration).

2. Landmark Formulation — Satyabrata Ghose (1954):
Mukherjea J. ruled that "impossibility" under Section 56 is not confined to physical impossibility, but includes circumstances where performance becomes commercially impracticable or fundamentally different from what was contemplated.

3. Recognized Grounds of Frustration:
(a) Destruction of Subject Matter (Taylor v. Caldwell — music hall burnt down).
(b) Death or Personal Incapacity in personal service contracts (Robinson v. Davison).
(c) Non-occurrence of Contemplated Event (Krell v. Henry — Coronation procession cancelled).
(d) Change of Law or Government Intervention.
(e) Outbreak of War.

4. Exceptions (No Frustration):
- Mere commercial hardship, price escalation, or difficulty of performance.
- Self-induced frustration or neglect.
- Default by a third party on whom the promisor relied.

5. Legal Consequence:
Under Section 65, any person who received any advantage under such void contract is bound to restore it or make compensation to the person from whom it was received.

6. Conclusion:
Section 56 discharges both parties from future obligations, automatically terminating the contract upon the occurrence of a supervening frustrating event.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Explain the "Golden Triangle" of Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Explain the "Golden Triangle" of Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Introduction: Articles 14 (Equality), 19 (Basic Freedoms), and 21 (Right to Life & Personal Liberty) form the "Golden Triangle" of the Indian Constitution.
2. Doctrinal Shift: Earlier in A.K. Gopalan (1950), the Supreme Court held these articles were mutually exclusive compartments. This was overruled in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978).
3. Interconnection: In Maneka Gandhi, Bhagwati J. ruled that a law depriving a person of life or personal liberty under Article 21 must also satisfy the test of Article 19 (reasonable restrictions) and Article 14 (non-arbitrariness). The "procedure established by law" must be "just, fair, and reasonable" and not whimsical.
4. Conclusion: The Golden Triangle serves as the foundational bulwark against arbitrary executive and legislative action, infusing substantive due process into Indian constitutional jurisprudence.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Discuss the scope and grounds of judicial review of Constitutional Amendments under the Basic Structure Doctrine.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Discuss the scope and grounds of judicial review of Constitutional Amendments under the Basic Structure Doctrine. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Introduction:
Article 368 empowers Parliament to amend the Constitution. However, this power is constituent and plenary, not unlimited. The Basic Structure Doctrine acts as an implied constitutional limitation to preserve core democratic principles.

2. Historical Evolution:
- Shankari Prasad (1951) & Sajjan Singh (1965): Upheld absolute parliamentary power under Article 368.
- Golaknath (1967): Held Parliament cannot abridge Fundamental Rights under Part III.
- 24th Amendment (1971): Parliament amended Art 13 & 368 to assert unrestricted power.

3. Landmark Ruling — Kesavananda Bharati (1973):

The Basic Structure Doctrine maintains constitutional equilibrium, ensuring Parliament cannot use its amendatory power to subvert constitutional democracy.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Examine the scope of Right to Equality under Article 14 of the Constitution. Distinguish between Reasonable Classification Test and the Doctrine of Non-Arbitrariness.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Examine the scope of Right to Equality under Article 14 of the Constitution. Distinguish between Reasonable Classification Test and the Doctrine of Non-Arbitrariness. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Introduction & Constitutional Framework:
Article 14 declares that "The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India."
- Equality before Law: A negative concept borrowed from English Common Law, implying absence of special privilege.
- Equal Protection of Laws: A positive concept borrowed from the 14th Amendment of the US Constitution, requiring equal treatment under equal circumstances ("equals must be treated equally, unequals cannot be treated equally").

2. Traditional Doctrine: Reasonable Classification:
Since absolute equality among unequal persons creates inequality, Article 14 permits legislative classification. In State of W.B. v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952) and Ram Krishna Dalmia (1958), the Supreme Court established the two-fold test:
(i) Intelligible Differentia: The classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia distinguishing persons or things grouped together from others left out.
(ii) Rational Nexus: The differentia must have a rational relation/nexus to the object sought to be achieved by the statute.

3. The Modern Dimension: Doctrine of Non-Arbitrariness:
In E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974), Bhagwati J. revolutionized Article 14 jurisprudence:
"Equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects and dimensions... Equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies; one belongs to the rule of law in a republic while the other, to the whim and caprice of an absolute monarch."
This was affirmed in Maneka Gandhi (1978) and Ramana Dayaram Shetty (1979).

4. Evolution into "Manifest Arbitrariness":
In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court held that "manifest arbitrariness" is a valid constitutional ground to strike down even primary legislation. A law is manifestly arbitrary if enacted without adequate determining principle or is excessively disproportionate, unreasonable, or capricious.

5. Comparison between Classification and Arbitrariness:
- Classification is a formulaic tool to assess statutory boundaries.
- Non-arbitrariness is the substantive core of Rule of Law ensuring fairness in state action.

6. Conclusion:
Article 14 has progressed from a formalistic classification test into an activist, substantive guarantee against unfairness, executive caprice, and legislative oppression.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Problem Question: The State Government issues an executive notification reserving 80% of management quota seats in private unaided law colleges exclusively for students domiciled in Gujarat. A meritorious student from Rajasthan challenging this notification claims violation of Articles 14, 15, and 19(1)(g). Decide using the IRAC method.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Problem Question: The State Government issues an executive notification reserving 80% of management quota seats in private unaided law colleges exclusively for students domiciled in Gujarat. A meritorious student from Rajasthan challenging this notification claims violation of Articles 14, 15, and 19(1)(g). Decide using the IRAC method. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
LEGAL PROBLEM ANALYSIS (IRAC METHOD)

1. ISSUES:
(a) Whether an 80% institutional/domicile quota in private unaided professional colleges violates the Right to Equality under Article 14.
(b) Whether the State executive notification impermissibly infringes the private colleges' right to occupation under Article 19(1)(g).
(c) Whether the Rajasthan petitioner is entitled to relief.

2. RELEVANT RULES & CONSTITUTIONAL PRINCIPLES:
- Article 14: Prohibits arbitrary state classification lacking rational nexus.
- Article 19(1)(g): Protects freedom to practice any profession or carry on any occupation/trade.
- P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005): A 7-judge bench ruled that the State cannot impose reservation policy or quota system on private unaided educational institutions.
- Dr. Pradeep Jain v. Union of India (1984): Excessive domicile reservation destroying merit violates Article 14.

3. APPLICATION TO FACTS:
- The private law colleges are unaided institutions. Under the P.A. Inamdar precedent, the state has no authority to commandeer 80% seats under an executive order.
- Furthermore, an 80% domicile reservation is excessively disproportionate and fails the rational nexus test, virtually barring outside meritorious candidates.
- Domicile preference cannot exceed reasonable ceilings (as held in Pradeep Jain).

4. CONCLUSION:
The executive notification is ultra vires Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The petition of the candidate from Rajasthan will succeed, and the 80% domicile quota must be quashed.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: What is a "Cross Offer"? Does it result in a binding contract?
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: What is a "Cross Offer"? Does it result in a binding contract? (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer: A Cross Offer occurs when two parties make identical offers to each other in ignorance of the other's offer simultaneously. Cross offers do not constitute acceptance of each other because there is no consensus ad idem (meeting of minds). Hence, cross offers do not result in a binding contract (Tinn v. Hoffman & Co., 1873).

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Explain the doctrine of "Promissory Estoppel" in Indian Contract Law.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Explain the doctrine of "Promissory Estoppel" in Indian Contract Law. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Definition: Promissory Estoppel is an equitable doctrine providing that where one party makes a clear promise intending to create legal relations, and the other party acts upon it and alters their position, the promisor cannot go back on the promise.
2. Key Elements:
(a) Clear and unambiguous representation or promise.
(b) Reasonable reliance and alteration of position by the promisee.
(c) Inequity if promisor is permitted to resile.
3. Application to Government: In Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills (1979), Bhagwati J. held that promissory estoppel applies against the Government where executive promises induced citizens to set up industries or invest capital, unless overriding public interest justifies otherwise.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Discuss the Doctrine of Frustration of Contract under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. State the grounds and exceptions.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Discuss the Doctrine of Frustration of Contract under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. State the grounds and exceptions. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Statutory Framework:
Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act provides:
- An agreement to do an impossible act is void ab initio.
- A contract becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful after the contract is made without the default of the promisor (Supervening Impossibility / Frustration).

2. Landmark Formulation — Satyabrata Ghose (1954):
Mukherjea J. ruled that "impossibility" under Section 56 is not confined to physical impossibility, but includes circumstances where performance becomes commercially impracticable or fundamentally different from what was contemplated.

3. Recognized Grounds of Frustration:
(a) Destruction of Subject Matter (Taylor v. Caldwell — music hall burnt down).
(b) Death or Personal Incapacity in personal service contracts (Robinson v. Davison).
(c) Non-occurrence of Contemplated Event (Krell v. Henry — Coronation procession cancelled).
(d) Change of Law or Government Intervention.
(e) Outbreak of War.

4. Exceptions (No Frustration):
- Mere commercial hardship, price escalation, or difficulty of performance.
- Self-induced frustration or neglect.
- Default by a third party on whom the promisor relied.

5. Legal Consequence:
Under Section 65, any person who received any advantage under such void contract is bound to restore it or make compensation to the person from whom it was received.

6. Conclusion:
Section 56 discharges both parties from future obligations, automatically terminating the contract upon the occurrence of a supervening frustrating event.

examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer: Under Article 12, "State" includes: (1) The Government and Parliament of India, (2) The Government and Legislature of each State, (3) All local authorities (e.g., Municipalities, Panchayats), and (4) Other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India. In Ajay Hasia v. examPrepQuestion.questionText: Explain the "Golden Triangle" of Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Explain the "Golden Triangle" of Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Introduction: Articles 14 (Equality), 19 (Basic Freedoms), and 21 (Right to Life & Personal Liberty) form the "Golden Triangle" of the Indian Constitution.
2. Doctrinal Shift: Earlier in A.K. Gopalan (1950), the Supreme Court held these articles were mutually exclusive compartments. This was overruled in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978).
3. Interconnection: In Maneka Gandhi, Bhagwati J. ruled that a law depriving a person of life or personal liberty under Article 21 must also satisfy the test of Article 19 (reasonable restrictions) and Article 14 (non-arbitrariness). The "procedure established by law" must be "just, fair, and reasonable" and not whimsical.
4. Conclusion: The Golden Triangle serves as the foundational bulwark against arbitrary executive and legislative action, infusing substantive due process into Indian constitutional jurisprudence.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Discuss the scope and grounds of judicial review of Constitutional Amendments under the Basic Structure Doctrine.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Discuss the scope and grounds of judicial review of Constitutional Amendments under the Basic Structure Doctrine. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Introduction:
Article 368 empowers Parliament to amend the Constitution. However, this power is constituent and plenary, not unlimited. The Basic Structure Doctrine acts as an implied constitutional limitation to preserve core democratic principles.

2. Historical Evolution:
- Shankari Prasad (1951) & Sajjan Singh (1965): Upheld absolute parliamentary power under Article 368.
- Golaknath (1967): Held Parliament cannot abridge Fundamental Rights under Part III.
- 24th Amendment (1971): Parliament amended Art 13 & 368 to assert unrestricted power.

3. Landmark Ruling — Kesavananda Bharati (1973):
A 13-judge bench held by 7:6 majority that while Parliament can amend any provision of the Constitution, including Part III, it cannot alter, abrogate, or destroy the "Basic Structure" of the Constitution.

4. Recognized Basic Features:
(a) Supremacy of the Constitution
(b) Republican and Democratic form of Government
(c) Secular character of the Constitution
(d) Separation of Powers between Legislature, Executive, and Judiciary
(e) Federal character of the Constitution
(f) Judicial Review (L. Chandra Kumar, 1997)
(g) Harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles (Minerva Mills, 1980)

5. Subsequent Affirmations:
In Minerva Mills (1980), clauses (4) and (5) of Art 368 were struck down. In the NJAC Case (2015), the 99th Constitutional Amendment was nullified because it compromised judicial independence.

6. Conclusion:
The Basic Structure Doctrine maintains constitutional equilibrium, ensuring Parliament cannot use its amendatory power to subvert constitutional democracy.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Examine the scope of Right to Equality under Article 14 of the Constitution. Distinguish between Reasonable Classification Test and the Doctrine of Non-Arbitrariness.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Examine the scope of Right to Equality under Article 14 of the Constitution. Distinguish between Reasonable Classification Test and the Doctrine of Non-Arbitrariness. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Introduction & Constitutional Framework:
Article 14 declares that "The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India."
- Equality before Law: A negative concept borrowed from English Common Law, implying absence of special privilege.
- Equal Protection of Laws: A positive concept borrowed from the 14th Amendment of the US Constitution, requiring equal treatment under equal circumstances ("equals must be treated equally, unequals cannot be treated equally").

2. Traditional Doctrine: Reasonable Classification:
Since absolute equality among unequal persons creates inequality, Article 14 permits legislative classification. In State of W.B. v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952) and Ram Krishna Dalmia (1958), the Supreme Court established the two-fold test:
(i) Intelligible Differentia: The classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia distinguishing persons or things grouped together from others left out.
(ii) Rational Nexus: The differentia must have a rational relation/nexus to the object sought to be achieved by the statute.

3. The Modern Dimension: Doctrine of Non-Arbitrariness:
In E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974), Bhagwati J. revolutionized Article 14 jurisprudence:
"Equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects and dimensions... Equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies; one belongs to the rule of law in a republic while the other, to the whim and caprice of an absolute monarch."
This was affirmed in Maneka Gandhi (1978) and Ramana Dayaram Shetty (1979).

4. Evolution into "Manifest Arbitrariness":
In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court held that "manifest arbitrariness" is a valid constitutional ground to strike down even primary legislation. A law is manifestly arbitrary if enacted without adequate determining principle or is excessively disproportionate, unreasonable, or capricious.

5. Comparison between Classification and Arbitrariness:
- Classification is a formulaic tool to assess statutory boundaries.
- Non-arbitrariness is the substantive core of Rule of Law ensuring fairness in state action.

6. Conclusion:
Article 14 has progressed from a formalistic classification test into an activist, substantive guarantee against unfairness, executive caprice, and legislative oppression.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Problem Question: The State Government issues an executive notification reserving 80% of management quota seats in private unaided law colleges exclusively for students domiciled in Gujarat. A meritorious student from Rajasthan challenging this notification claims violation of Articles 14, 15, and 19(1)(g). Decide using the IRAC method.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Problem Question: The State Government issues an executive notification reserving 80% of management quota seats in private unaided law colleges exclusively for students domiciled in Gujarat. A meritorious student from Rajasthan challenging this notification claims violation of Articles 14, 15, and 19(1)(g). Decide using the IRAC method. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
LEGAL PROBLEM ANALYSIS (IRAC METHOD)

1. ISSUES:
(a) Whether an 80% institutional/domicile quota in private unaided professional colleges violates the Right to Equality under Article 14.
(b) Whether the State executive notification impermissibly infringes the private colleges' right to occupation under Article 19(1)(g).
(c) Whether the Rajasthan petitioner is entitled to relief.

2. RELEVANT RULES & CONSTITUTIONAL PRINCIPLES:
- Article 14: Prohibits arbitrary state classification lacking rational nexus.
- Article 19(1)(g): Protects freedom to practice any profession or carry on any occupation/trade.
- P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005): A 7-judge bench ruled that the State cannot impose reservation policy or quota system on private unaided educational institutions.
- Dr. Pradeep Jain v. Union of India (1984): Excessive domicile reservation destroying merit violates Article 14.

3. APPLICATION TO FACTS:
- The private law colleges are unaided institutions. Under the P.A. Inamdar precedent, the state has no authority to commandeer 80% seats under an executive order.
- Furthermore, an 80% domicile reservation is excessively disproportionate and fails the rational nexus test, virtually barring outside meritorious candidates.
- Domicile preference cannot exceed reasonable ceilings (as held in Pradeep Jain).

4. CONCLUSION:
The executive notification is ultra vires Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The petition of the candidate from Rajasthan will succeed, and the 80% domicile quota must be quashed.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: What is a "Cross Offer"? Does it result in a binding contract?
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: What is a "Cross Offer"? Does it result in a binding contract? (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer: A Cross Offer occurs when two parties make identical offers to each other in ignorance of the other's offer simultaneously. Cross offers do not constitute acceptance of each other because there is no consensus ad idem (meeting of minds). Hence, cross offers do not result in a binding contract (Tinn v. Hoffman & Co., 1873).

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Explain the doctrine of "Promissory Estoppel" in Indian Contract Law.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Explain the doctrine of "Promissory Estoppel" in Indian Contract Law. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Definition: Promissory Estoppel is an equitable doctrine providing that where one party makes a clear promise intending to create legal relations, and the other party acts upon it and alters their position, the promisor cannot go back on the promise.
2. Key Elements:
(a) Clear and unambiguous representation or promise.
(b) Reasonable reliance and alteration of position by the promisee.
(c) Inequity if promisor is permitted to resile.
3. Application to Government: In Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills (1979), Bhagwati J. held that promissory estoppel applies against the Government where executive promises induced citizens to set up industries or invest capital, unless overriding public interest justifies otherwise.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Discuss the Doctrine of Frustration of Contract under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. State the grounds and exceptions.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Discuss the Doctrine of Frustration of Contract under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. State the grounds and exceptions. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Statutory Framework:
Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act provides:
- An agreement to do an impossible act is void ab initio.
- A contract becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful after the contract is made without the default of the promisor (Supervening Impossibility / Frustration).

2. Landmark Formulation — Satyabrata Ghose (1954):
Mukherjea J. ruled that "impossibility" under Section 56 is not confined to physical impossibility, but includes circumstances where performance becomes commercially impracticable or fundamentally different from what was contemplated.

3. Recognized Grounds of Frustration:
(a) Destruction of Subject Matter (Taylor v. Caldwell — music hall burnt down).
(b) Death or Personal Incapacity in personal service contracts (Robinson v. Davison).
(c) Non-occurrence of Contemplated Event (Krell v. Henry — Coronation procession cancelled).
(d) Change of Law or Government Intervention.
(e) Outbreak of War.

4. Exceptions (No Frustration):
- Mere commercial hardship, price escalation, or difficulty of performance.
- Self-induced frustration or neglect.
- Default by a third party on whom the promisor relied.

5. Legal Consequence:
Under Section 65, any person who received any advantage under such void contract is bound to restore it or make compensation to the person from whom it was received.

6. Conclusion:
Section 56 discharges both parties from future obligations, automatically terminating the contract upon the occurrence of a supervening frustrating event.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Define "State" under Article 12 of the Constitution of India.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Define "State" under Article 12 of the Constitution of India. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer: Under Article 12, "State" includes: (1) The Government and Parliament of India, (2) The Government and Legislature of each State, (3) All local authorities (e.g., Municipalities, Panchayats), and (4) Other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India. In Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib, the Supreme Court laid down that if a body is financially, functionally, and administratively dominated by the Government, it is an instrumentality of the State under Article 12.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: What is the "Doctrine of Severability" under Article 13(1)?
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: What is the "Doctrine of Severability" under Article 13(1)? (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer: The Doctrine of Severability (Art 13) provides that when a statute violates fundamental rights, only the unconstitutional portion is void, provided the valid and invalid portions are separable. If the valid part can independently survive and operate without the invalid portion, the court will uphold the valid part (A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras; R.M.D.C. v. Union of India).

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Explain the "Golden Triangle" of Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Explain the "Golden Triangle" of Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Introduction: Articles 14 (Equality), 19 (Basic Freedoms), and 21 (Right to Life & Personal Liberty) form the "Golden Triangle" of the Indian Constitution.
2. Doctrinal Shift: Earlier in A.K. Gopalan (1950), the Supreme Court held these articles were mutually exclusive compartments. This was overruled in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978).
3. Interconnection: In Maneka Gandhi, Bhagwati J. ruled that a law depriving a person of life or personal liberty under Article 21 must also satisfy the test of Article 19 (reasonable restrictions) and Article 14 (non-arbitrariness). The "procedure established by law" must be "just, fair, and reasonable" and not whimsical.
4. Conclusion: The Golden Triangle serves as the foundational bulwark against arbitrary executive and legislative action, infusing substantive due process into Indian constitutional jurisprudence.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Discuss the scope and grounds of judicial review of Constitutional Amendments under the Basic Structure Doctrine.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Discuss the scope and grounds of judicial review of Constitutional Amendments under the Basic Structure Doctrine. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Introduction:
Article 368 empowers Parliament to amend the Constitution. However, this power is constituent and plenary, not unlimited. The Basic Structure Doctrine acts as an implied constitutional limitation to preserve core democratic principles.

2. Historical Evolution:
- Shankari Prasad (1951) & Sajjan Singh (1965): Upheld absolute parliamentary power under Article 368.
- Golaknath (1967): Held Parliament cannot abridge Fundamental Rights under Part III.
- 24th Amendment (1971): Parliament amended Art 13 & 368 to assert unrestricted power.

3. Landmark Ruling — Kesavananda Bharati (1973):
A 13-judge bench held by 7:6 majority that while Parliament can amend any provision of the Constitution, including Part III, it cannot alter, abrogate, or destroy the "Basic Structure" of the Constitution.

4. Recognized Basic Features:
(a) Supremacy of the Constitution
(b) Republican and Democratic form of Government
(c) Secular character of the Constitution
(d) Separation of Powers between Legislature, Executive, and Judiciary
(e) Federal character of the Constitution
(f) Judicial Review (L. Chandra Kumar, 1997)
(g) Harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles (Minerva Mills, 1980)

5. Subsequent Affirmations:
In Minerva Mills (1980), clauses (4) and (5) of Art 368 were struck down. In the NJAC Case (2015), the 99th Constitutional Amendment was nullified because it compromised judicial independence.

6. Conclusion:
The Basic Structure Doctrine maintains constitutional equilibrium, ensuring Parliament cannot use its amendatory power to subvert constitutional democracy.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Examine the scope of Right to Equality under Article 14 of the Constitution. Distinguish between Reasonable Classification Test and the Doctrine of Non-Arbitrariness.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Examine the scope of Right to Equality under Article 14 of the Constitution. Distinguish between Reasonable Classification Test and the Doctrine of Non-Arbitrariness. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Introduction & Constitutional Framework:
Article 14 declares that "The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India."
- Equality before Law: A negative concept borrowed from English Common Law, implying absence of special privilege.
- Equal Protection of Laws: A positive concept borrowed from the 14th Amendment of the US Constitution, requiring equal treatment under equal circumstances ("equals must be treated equally, unequals cannot be treated equally").

2. Traditional Doctrine: Reasonable Classification:
Since absolute equality among unequal persons creates inequality, Article 14 permits legislative classification. In State of W.B. v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952) and Ram Krishna Dalmia (1958), the Supreme Court established the two-fold test:
(i) Intelligible Differentia: The classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia distinguishing persons or things grouped together from others left out.
(ii) Rational Nexus: The differentia must have a rational relation/nexus to the object sought to be achieved by the statute.

3. The Modern Dimension: Doctrine of Non-Arbitrariness:
In E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974), Bhagwati J. revolutionized Article 14 jurisprudence:
"Equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects and dimensions... Equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies; one belongs to the rule of law in a republic while the other, to the whim and caprice of an absolute monarch."
This was affirmed in Maneka Gandhi (1978) and Ramana Dayaram Shetty (1979).

4. Evolution into "Manifest Arbitrariness":
In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court held that "manifest arbitrariness" is a valid constitutional ground to strike down even primary legislation. A law is manifestly arbitrary if enacted without adequate determining principle or is excessively disproportionate, unreasonable, or capricious.

5. Comparison between Classification and Arbitrariness:
- Classification is a formulaic tool to assess statutory boundaries.
- Non-arbitrariness is the substantive core of Rule of Law ensuring fairness in state action.

6. Conclusion:
Article 14 has progressed from a formalistic classification test into an activist, substantive guarantee against unfairness, executive caprice, and legislative oppression.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Problem Question: The State Government issues an executive notification reserving 80% of management quota seats in private unaided law colleges exclusively for students domiciled in Gujarat. A meritorious student from Rajasthan challenging this notification claims violation of Articles 14, 15, and 19(1)(g). Decide using the IRAC method.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Problem Question: The State Government issues an executive notification reserving 80% of management quota seats in private unaided law colleges exclusively for students domiciled in Gujarat. A meritorious student from Rajasthan challenging this notification claims violation of Articles 14, 15, and 19(1)(g). Decide using the IRAC method. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
LEGAL PROBLEM ANALYSIS (IRAC METHOD)

1. ISSUES:
(a) Whether an 80% institutional/domicile quota in private unaided professional colleges violates the Right to Equality under Article 14.
(b) Whether the State executive notification impermissibly infringes the private colleges' right to occupation under Article 19(1)(g).
(c) Whether the Rajasthan petitioner is entitled to relief.

2. RELEVANT RULES & CONSTITUTIONAL PRINCIPLES:
- Article 14: Prohibits arbitrary state classification lacking rational nexus.
- Article 19(1)(g): Protects freedom to practice any profession or carry on any occupation/trade.
- P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005): A 7-judge bench ruled that the State cannot impose reservation policy or quota system on private unaided educational institutions.
- Dr. Pradeep Jain v. Union of India (1984): Excessive domicile reservation destroying merit violates Article 14.

3. APPLICATION TO FACTS:
- The private law colleges are unaided institutions. Under the P.A. Inamdar precedent, the state has no authority to commandeer 80% seats under an executive order.
- Furthermore, an 80% domicile reservation is excessively disproportionate and fails the rational nexus test, virtually barring outside meritorious candidates.
- Domicile preference cannot exceed reasonable ceilings (as held in Pradeep Jain).

4. CONCLUSION:
The executive notification is ultra vires Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The petition of the candidate from Rajasthan will succeed, and the 80% domicile quota must be quashed.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: What is a "Cross Offer"? Does it result in a binding contract?

examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer: A Cross Offer occurs when two parties make identical offers to each other in ignorance of the other's offer simultaneously. Cross offers do not constitute acceptance of each other because there is no consensus ad idem (meeting of minds). Hence, cross offers do not result in a binding contract (Tinn v. Hoffman & Co., 1873).

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Explain the doctrine of "Promissory Estoppel" in Indian Contract Law.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Explain the doctrine of "Promissory Estoppel" in Indian Contract Law. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Definition: Promissory Estoppel is an equitable doctrine providing that where one party makes a clear promise intending to create legal relations, and the other party acts upon it and alters their position, the promisor cannot go back on the promise.
2. Key Elements:
(a) Clear and unambiguous representation or promise.
(b) Reasonable reliance and alteration of position by the promisee.
(c) Inequity if promisor is permitted to resile.
3. Application to Government: In Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills (1979), Bhagwati J. held that promissory estoppel applies against the Government where executive promises induced citizens to set up industries or invest capital, unless overriding public interest justifies otherwise.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Discuss the Doctrine of Frustration of Contract under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. State the grounds and exceptions.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Discuss the Doctrine of Frustration of Contract under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. State the grounds and exceptions. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Statutory Framework:
Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act provides:
- An agreement to do an impossible act is void ab initio.
- A contract becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful after the contract is made without the default of the promisor (Supervening Impossibility / Frustration).

2. Landmark Formulation — Satyabrata Ghose (1954):
Mukherjea J. ruled that "impossibility" under Section 56 is not confined to physical impossibility, but includes circumstances where performance becomes commercially impracticable or fundamentally different from what was contemplated.

3. Recognized Grounds of Frustration:
(a) Destruction of Subject Matter (Taylor v. Caldwell — music hall burnt down).
(b) Death or Personal Incapacity in personal service contracts (Robinson v. Davison).
(c) Non-occurrence of Contemplated Event (Krell v. Henry — Coronation procession cancelled).
(d) Change of Law or Government Intervention.
(e) Outbreak of War.

4. Exceptions (No Frustration):
- Mere commercial hardship, price escalation, or difficulty of performance.
- Self-induced frustration or neglect.
- Default by a third party on whom the promisor relied.

5. Legal Consequence:
Under Section 65, any person who received any advantage under such void contract is bound to restore it or make compensation to the person from whom it was received.

6. Conclusion:
Section 56 discharges both parties from future obligations, automatically terminating the contract upon the occurrence of a supervening frustrating event.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Explain the conditions precedent to Retrenchment of a workman under Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. What is the effect of non-compliance?
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Explain the conditions precedent to Retrenchment of a workman under Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. What is the effect of non-compliance? (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Definition & Scope:
Under Section 2(oo) of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, "Retrenchment" means the termination by the employer of the service of a workman for any reason whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by disciplinary action (excluding voluntary retirement, superannuation, or termination due to continuous ill-health).

2. Applicability (Section 25B):
Section 25F protects any workman who has been in "continuous service for not less than one year" (which under Sec 25B means 240 days of actual work in the preceding 12 months).

3. Mandatory Conditions Precedent (Section 25F):
No workman can be retrenched until:
(a) Notice: The workman has been given one month's notice in writing indicating the reasons for retrenchment, or the workman has been paid wages in lieu of such notice.
(b) Retrenchment Compensation: The workman has been paid compensation equivalent to 15 days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service or any part thereof in excess of six months.
(c) Government Notice: Notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate government or specified authority.

4. Simultaneous Payment Rule:
Compensation and notice pay must be tendered simultaneously at the time of retrenchment (SBI v. N. Sundara Money).

5. Legal Effect of Non-Compliance:
In Pramod Jha v. State of Bihar (2003) and Anoop Sharma (2010), the Supreme Court affirmed that Section 25F conditions are mandatory conditions precedent. Non-compliance renders the retrenchment order void ab initio (a nullity in law), entitling the workman to reinstatement with continuity of service and back wages.

6. Conclusion:
Section 25F provides vital social security against arbitrary retrenchment, mandating strict statutory compliance before termination.

examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer: In Bangalore Water Supply v. A. Profit motive is irrelevant; only strictly sovereign functions are excluded.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Explain the conditions precedent to Retrenchment of a workman under Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. What is the effect of non-compliance?
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Explain the conditions precedent to Retrenchment of a workman under Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. What is the effect of non-compliance? (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Definition & Scope:
Under Section 2(oo) of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, "Retrenchment" means the termination by the employer of the service of a workman for any reason whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by disciplinary action (excluding voluntary retirement, superannuation, or termination due to continuous ill-health).

2. Applicability (Section 25B):
Section 25F protects any workman who has been in "continuous service for not less than one year" (which under Sec 25B means 240 days of actual work in the preceding 12 months).

3. Mandatory Conditions Precedent (Section 25F):
No workman can be retrenched until:
(a) Notice: The workman has been given one month's notice in writing indicating the reasons for retrenchment, or the workman has been paid wages in lieu of such notice.
(b) Retrenchment Compensation: The workman has been paid compensation equivalent to 15 days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service or any part thereof in excess of six months.
(c) Government Notice: Notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate government or specified authority.

4. Simultaneous Payment Rule:
Compensation and notice pay must be tendered simultaneously at the time of retrenchment (SBI v. N. Sundara Money).

5. Legal Effect of Non-Compliance:
In Pramod Jha v. State of Bihar (2003) and Anoop Sharma (2010), the Supreme Court affirmed that Section 25F conditions are mandatory conditions precedent. Non-compliance renders the retrenchment order void ab initio (a nullity in law), entitling the workman to reinstatement with continuity of service and back wages.

6. Conclusion:
Section 25F provides vital social security against arbitrary retrenchment, mandating strict statutory compliance before termination.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Define "Industry" under Section 2(j) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 as per the Bangalore Water Supply case.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Define "Industry" under Section 2(j) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 as per the Bangalore Water Supply case. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer: In Bangalore Water Supply v. A. Rajappa (1978), the Supreme Court laid down the "Triple Test" for Section 2(j): An activity is an "Industry" if there is (1) Systematic activity, (2) Organized by cooperation between employer and employee, and (3) For the production and/or distribution of goods and services calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes. Profit motive is irrelevant; only strictly sovereign functions are excluded.

Under Section 2(oo) of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, "Retrenchment" means the termination by the employer of the service of a workman for any reason whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by disciplinary action (excluding voluntary retirement, superannuation, or termination due to continuous ill-health).

2. Applicability (Section 25B):
Section 25F protects any workman who has been in "continuous service for not less than one year" (which under Sec 25B means 240 days of actual work in the preceding 12 months).

3. Mandatory Conditions Precedent (Section 25F):
No workman can be retrenched until:
(a) Notice: The workman has been given one month's notice in writing indicating the reasons for retrenchment, or the workman has been paid wages in lieu of such notice.
(b) Retrenchment Compensation: The workman has been paid compensation equivalent to 15 days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service or any part thereof in excess of six months.
(c) Government Notice: Notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate government or specified authority.

4. Simultaneous Payment Rule:
Compensation and notice pay must be tendered simultaneously at the time of retrenchment (SBI v. N. Sundara Money).

5. Legal Effect of Non-Compliance:
In Pramod Jha v. State of Bihar (2003) and Anoop Sharma (2010), the Supreme Court affirmed that Section 25F conditions are mandatory conditions precedent. Non-compliance renders the retrenchment order void ab initio (a nullity in law), entitling the workman to reinstatement with continuity of service and back wages.

6. Conclusion:
Section 25F provides vital social security against arbitrary retrenchment, mandating strict statutory compliance before termination.

examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer: In Bangalore Water Supply v. A. Rajappa (1978), the Supreme Court laid down the "Triple Test" for Section 2(j): An activity is an "Industry" if there is (1) Systematic activity, (2) Organized by cooperation between employer and employee, and (3) For the production and/or distribution of goods and services calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes. Profit motive is irrelevant; only strictly sovereign functions are excluded.

examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Explain the conditions precedent to Retrenchment of a workman under Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. What is the effect of non-compliance? (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Definition & Scope:
Under Section 2(oo) of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, "Retrenchment" means the termination by the employer of the service of a workman for any reason whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by disciplinary action (excluding voluntary retirement, superannuation, or termination due to continuous ill-health).

2. Applicability (Section 25B):
Section 25F protects any workman who has been in "continuous service for not less than one year" (which under Sec 25B means 240 days of actual work in the preceding 12 months).

3. Mandatory Conditions Precedent (Section 25F):
No workman can be retrenched until:
(a) Notice: The workman has been given one month's notice in writing indicating the reasons for retrenchment, or the workman has been paid wages in lieu of such notice.
(b) Retrenchment Compensation: The workman has been paid compensation equivalent to 15 days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service or any part thereof in excess of six months.
(c) Government Notice: Notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate government or specified authority.

4. Simultaneous Payment Rule:
Compensation and notice pay must be tendered simultaneously at the time of retrenchment (SBI v. N. Sundara Money).

5. Legal Effect of Non-Compliance:
In Pramod Jha v. State of Bihar (2003) and Anoop Sharma (2010), the Supreme Court affirmed that Section 25F conditions are mandatory conditions precedent. Non-compliance renders the retrenchment order void ab initio (a nullity in law), entitling the workman to reinstatement with continuity of service and back wages.

6. Conclusion:
Section 25F provides vital social security against arbitrary retrenchment, mandating strict statutory compliance before termination.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Define "State" under Article 12 of the Constitution of India.

examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer: Under Article 12, "State" includes: (1) The Government and Parliament of India, (2) The Government and Legislature of each State, (3) All local authorities (e.g., Municipalities, Panchayats), and (4) Other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India. examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer: The Doctrine of Severability (Art 13) provides that when a statute violates fundamental rights, only the unconstitutional portion is void, provided the valid and invalid portions are separable. If the valid part can independently survive and operate without the invalid portion, the court will uphold the valid part (A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras; R.M.D.C. v. Union of India).

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Explain the "Golden Triangle" of Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Explain the "Golden Triangle" of Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Introduction: Articles 14 (Equality), 19 (Basic Freedoms), and 21 (Right to Life & Personal Liberty) form the "Golden Triangle" of the Indian Constitution.
2. Doctrinal Shift: Earlier in A.K. Gopalan (1950), the Supreme Court held these articles were mutually exclusive compartments. This was overruled in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978).
3. Interconnection: In Maneka Gandhi, Bhagwati J. ruled that a law depriving a person of life or personal liberty under Article 21 must also satisfy the test of Article 19 (reasonable restrictions) and Article 14 (non-arbitrariness). The "procedure established by law" must be "just, fair, and reasonable" and not whimsical.
4. Conclusion: The Golden Triangle serves as the foundational bulwark against arbitrary executive and legislative action, infusing substantive due process into Indian constitutional jurisprudence.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Discuss the scope and grounds of judicial review of Constitutional Amendments under the Basic Structure Doctrine.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Discuss the scope and grounds of judicial review of Constitutional Amendments under the Basic Structure Doctrine. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Introduction:
Article 368 empowers Parliament to amend the Constitution. However, this power is constituent and plenary, not unlimited. The Basic Structure Doctrine acts as an implied constitutional limitation to preserve core democratic principles.

2. Historical Evolution:
- Shankari Prasad (1951) & Sajjan Singh (1965): Upheld absolute parliamentary power under Article 368.
- Golaknath (1967): Held Parliament cannot abridge Fundamental Rights under Part III.
- 24th Amendment (1971): Parliament amended Art 13 & 368 to assert unrestricted power.

3. Landmark Ruling — Kesavananda Bharati (1973):
A 13-judge bench held by 7:6 majority that while Parliament can amend any provision of the Constitution, including Part III, it cannot alter, abrogate, or destroy the "Basic Structure" of the Constitution.

4. Recognized Basic Features:
(a) Supremacy of the Constitution
(b) Republican and Democratic form of Government
(c) Secular character of the Constitution
(d) Separation of Powers between Legislature, Executive, and Judiciary
(e) Federal character of the Constitution
(f) Judicial Review (L. Chandra Kumar, 1997)
(g) Harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles (Minerva Mills, 1980)

5. Subsequent Affirmations:
In Minerva Mills (1980), clauses (4) and (5) of Art 368 were struck down. In the NJAC Case (2015), the 99th Constitutional Amendment was nullified because it compromised judicial independence.

6. Conclusion:
The Basic Structure Doctrine maintains constitutional equilibrium, ensuring Parliament cannot use its amendatory power to subvert constitutional democracy.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Examine the scope of Right to Equality under Article 14 of the Constitution. Distinguish between Reasonable Classification Test and the Doctrine of Non-Arbitrariness.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Examine the scope of Right to Equality under Article 14 of the Constitution. Distinguish between Reasonable Classification Test and the Doctrine of Non-Arbitrariness. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Introduction & Constitutional Framework:
Article 14 declares that "The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India."
- Equality before Law: A negative concept borrowed from English Common Law, implying absence of special privilege.
- Equal Protection of Laws: A positive concept borrowed from the 14th Amendment of the US Constitution, requiring equal treatment under equal circumstances ("equals must be treated equally, unequals cannot be treated equally").

2. Traditional Doctrine: Reasonable Classification:
Since absolute equality among unequal persons creates inequality, Article 14 permits legislative classification. In State of W.B. v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952) and Ram Krishna Dalmia (1958), the Supreme Court established the two-fold test:
(i) Intelligible Differentia: The classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia distinguishing persons or things grouped together from others left out.
(ii) Rational Nexus: The differentia must have a rational relation/nexus to the object sought to be achieved by the statute.

3. The Modern Dimension: Doctrine of Non-Arbitrariness:
In E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974), Bhagwati J. revolutionized Article 14 jurisprudence:
"Equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects and dimensions... Equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies; one belongs to the rule of law in a republic while the other, to the whim and caprice of an absolute monarch."
This was affirmed in Maneka Gandhi (1978) and Ramana Dayaram Shetty (1979).

4. Evolution into "Manifest Arbitrariness":
In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court held that "manifest arbitrariness" is a valid constitutional ground to strike down even primary legislation. A law is manifestly arbitrary if enacted without adequate determining principle or is excessively disproportionate, unreasonable, or capricious.

5. Comparison between Classification and Arbitrariness:
- Classification is a formulaic tool to assess statutory boundaries.
- Non-arbitrariness is the substantive core of Rule of Law ensuring fairness in state action.

6. Conclusion:
Article 14 has progressed from a formalistic classification test into an activist, substantive guarantee against unfairness, executive caprice, and legislative oppression.

Article 14 declares that "The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India."

- Equal Protection of Laws: A positive concept borrowed from the 14th Amendment of the US Constitution, requiring equal treatment under equal circumstances ("equals must be treated equally, unequals cannot be treated equally").

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Problem Question: The State Government issues an executive notification reserving 80% of management quota seats in private unaided law colleges exclusively for students domiciled in Gujarat. A meritorious student from Rajasthan challenging this notification claims violation of Articles 14, 15, and 19(1)(g). Decide using the IRAC method.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Problem Question: The State Government issues an executive notification reserving 80% of management quota seats in private unaided law colleges exclusively for students domiciled in Gujarat. A meritorious student from Rajasthan challenging this notification claims violation of Articles 14, 15, and 19(1)(g). Decide using the IRAC method. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
LEGAL PROBLEM ANALYSIS (IRAC METHOD)

1. ISSUES:
(a) Whether an 80% institutional/domicile quota in private unaided professional colleges violates the Right to Equality under Article 14.
(b) Whether the State executive notification impermissibly infringes the private colleges' right to occupation under Article 19(1)(g).
(c) Whether the Rajasthan petitioner is entitled to relief.

2. RELEVANT RULES & CONSTITUTIONAL PRINCIPLES:
- Article 14: Prohibits arbitrary state classification lacking rational nexus.
- Article 19(1)(g): Protects freedom to practice any profession or carry on any occupation/trade.
- P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005): A 7-judge bench ruled that the State cannot impose reservation policy or quota system on private unaided educational institutions.
- Dr. Pradeep Jain v. Union of India (1984): Excessive domicile reservation destroying merit violates Article 14.

3. APPLICATION TO FACTS:
- The private law colleges are unaided institutions. Under the P.A. Inamdar precedent, the state has no authority to commandeer 80% seats under an executive order.
- Furthermore, an 80% domicile reservation is excessively disproportionate and fails the rational nexus test, virtually barring outside meritorious candidates.
- Domicile preference cannot exceed reasonable ceilings (as held in Pradeep Jain).

4. CONCLUSION:
The executive notification is ultra vires Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The petition of the candidate from Rajasthan will succeed, and the 80% domicile quota must be quashed.

examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer: Section 4(f) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS 2023) introduces "Community Service" as a distinct form of punishment. examPrepQuestion.questionText: Explain the offence of "Terrorist Act" under Section 113 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS 2023).
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Explain the offence of "Terrorist Act" under Section 113 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS 2023). (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Statutory Framework: Section 113 of BNS 2023 incorporates the offence of "Terrorist Act" into general penal law.
2. Essential Elements: An act is a terrorist act if done with intent to threaten or likely to threaten the unity, integrity, sovereignty, security, or economic security of India, or with intent to strike terror in the people or any section thereof.
3. Means Employed: Using bombs, dynamite, firearms, lethal weapons, poisonous gases, radioactive materials, or destroying critical infrastructure/monetary stability.
4. Penal Sanctions:
- If the terrorist act results in death: Punishable with Death or Imprisonment for Life, and minimum fine of ₹10 Lakhs.
- In other cases: Imprisonment from 5 years up to Life Imprisonment, with fine.

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Distinguish between Murder (Section 101 BNS / Sec 300 IPC) and Culpable Homicide not amounting to Murder (Section 100 BNS / Sec 299 IPC) with landmark judicial tests.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Distinguish between Murder (Section 101 BNS / Sec 300 IPC) and Culpable Homicide not amounting to Murder (Section 100 BNS / Sec 299 IPC) with landmark judicial tests. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Genus vs Species Relationship:
All murders are culpable homicides, but all culpable homicides are not murder. Culpable homicide (Sec 100 BNS / Sec 299 IPC) is the genus, while Murder (Sec 101 BNS / Sec 300 IPC) is the species.

2. The Fundamental Distinction — Probability of Death:
In the classic ruling Reg. v. Govinda (1876), Melvill J. established that the line of demarcation depends upon the degree of risk to human life:

(A) Intention:
- Culpable Homicide (Sec 100): Intention to cause death OR intention to cause bodily injury likely to cause death.
- Murder (Sec 101): Intention to cause death OR intention to cause bodily injury which offender knows is likely to cause death OR intention to inflict bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death (Virsa Singh test).

(B) Knowledge:
- Culpable Homicide: Knowledge that the act is likely to cause death.
- Murder (4th Clause): Knowledge that the act is so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death, without any excuse.

3. The 5 Exceptions to Murder:
An act prima facie falling under Section 101 BNS is reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder if covered by any of the 5 exceptions:
(i) Grave and sudden provocation
(ii) Exceeding the right of private defence in good faith
(iii) Public servant exceeding lawful powers in good faith
(iv) Sudden fight in heat of passion without premeditation
(v) Victim above 18 years consenting to suffer death

4. Conclusion:
Culpable homicide is punishable under Sec 105 BNS (Imprisonment up to 10 yrs or Life), whereas Murder is punishable under Sec 103 BNS (Death or Life Imprisonment).

examPrepQuestion.questionText: What is a "Cross Offer"? Does it result in a binding contract?
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: What is a "Cross Offer"? Does it result in a binding contract? (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer: A Cross Offer occurs when two parties make identical offers to each other in ignorance of the other's offer simultaneously. Cross offers do not constitute acceptance of each other because there is no consensus ad idem (meeting of minds). Hence, cross offers do not result in a binding contract (Tinn v. Hoffman & Co., 1873).

examPrepQuestion.questionText: Explain the doctrine of "Promissory Estoppel" in Indian Contract Law.
examPrepQuestion.questionTextGu: Explain the doctrine of "Promissory Estoppel" in Indian Contract Law. (ગુજરાતી મોડેલ પ્રશ્ન)
examPrepQuestion.modelAnswer:
1. Definition: Promissory Estoppel is an equitable doctrine providing that where one party makes a clear promise intending to create legal relations, and the other party acts upon it and alters their position, the promisor cannot go back on the promise.
2. Key Elements:
(a) Clear and unambiguous representation or promise.
(b) Reasonable reliance and alteration of position by the promisee.
(c) Inequity if promisor is permitted to resile.
3. Application to Government: In Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills (1979), Bhagwati J. held that promissory estoppel applies against the Government where executive promises induced citizens to set up industries or invest capital, unless overriding public interest justifies otherwise.
